1. Curr Biol. 2007 Sep 18;17(18):1568-73. doi: 10.1016/j.cub.2007.07.063. Epub
2007  Aug 30.

TMS evidence for the involvement of the right occipital face area in early face 
processing.

Pitcher D(1), Walsh V, Yovel G, Duchaine B.

Author information:
(1)Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience, Department of Psychology, University 
College London, Alexandra House, 17 Queen Square, London WC1N 3AR, United 
Kingdom. d.pitcher@ucl.ac.uk

Comment in
    Curr Biol. 2007 Oct 23;17(20):R888-9. doi: 10.1016/j.cub.2007.08.008.

Extensive research has demonstrated that several specialized cortical regions 
respond preferentially to faces. One such region, located in the inferior 
occipital gyrus, has been dubbed the occipital face area (OFA). The OFA is the 
first stage in two influential face-processing models, both of which suggest 
that it constructs an initial representation of a face, but how and when it does 
so remains unclear. The present study revealed that repetitive transcranial 
magnetic stimulation (rTMS) targeted at the right OFA (rOFA) disrupted accurate 
discrimination of face parts but had no effect on the discrimination of spacing 
between these parts. rTMS to left OFA had no effect. A matched part and spacing 
discrimination task that used house stimuli showed no impairment. In a second 
experiment, rTMS to rOFA replicated the face-part impairment but did not produce 
the same effect in an adjacent area, the lateral occipital cortex. A third 
experiment delivered double pulses of TMS separated by 40 ms at six periods 
after stimulus presentation during face-part discrimination. Accuracy dropped 
when pulses were delivered at 60 and 100 ms only. These findings indicate that 
the rOFA processes face-part information at an early stage in the 
face-processing stream.
